topic: Single-phase immersion vs rear-door heat exchangers (RDHx) for high-density rack retrofits

docs.title: Open Thermal Benchmark Consortium — 2025 retrofit heat-rejection report
docs.snippet: Across the consortium's retrofit suite, rear-door heat exchangers sustained higher per-rack heat rejection at equal facility water flow than single-phase immersion…
docs.text: Across the consortium's retrofit test suite, rear-door heat exchangers (RDHx) sustained higher per-rack heat rejection at equal facility water flow than single-phase immersion systems, and the gap widened as rack density rose. The tradeoff is floor loading and hose management at the rack rear. Measurements were produced on the consortium's own instrumented test hall with its own data-acquisition harness.

docs.title: ETH Zürich Systems Lab — independent replication of the retrofit heat-rejection comparison
docs.snippet: We reproduced the RDHx vs immersion comparison on our own instrumented racks with a measurement rig we built ourselves rather than the consortium's harness…
docs.text: We reproduced the retrofit heat-rejection comparison on different hardware, using an instrumented rack rig and data-acquisition stack we built ourselves rather than the consortium's harness, so this is an independent measurement rather than a re-analysis. Our results agree with the consortium: RDHx sustained higher per-rack heat rejection at equal facility water flow than single-phase immersion in retrofit scenarios. We also confirm the floor-loading tradeoff.

docs.title: Helmholtz Data Centre Lab — measuring Calder's 40% cooling-energy claim
docs.snippet: …Calder Systems' claim that single-phase immersion cuts total cooling energy by 40% versus rear-door heat-exchanger retrofits…
docs.text: We attempted to reproduce Calder Systems' widely circulated claim that single-phase immersion cuts total cooling energy by 40% versus rear-door heat-exchanger retrofits. Across three rack configurations and two seasons we measured 9-14% savings. The 40% figure appears to assume free-cooling hours and pump curves that none of our sites could match. We conclude the figure is not transferable to typical retrofit conditions.

docs.title: Calder Systems whitepaper — the 40% energy case for immersion retrofits
docs.snippet: Our modeling shows single-phase immersion cuts total cooling energy by 40% versus rear-door heat-exchanger retrofits at typical densities…
docs.text: Calder Systems' modeling shows single-phase immersion cuts total cooling energy by roughly 40% versus rear-door heat-exchanger retrofits at typical AI-training densities. The model is built on our internal deployment telemetry and our reference pump curves; assumptions are listed in the appendix.

docs.title: Calder Systems engineering blog — inside our 40% modeling
docs.snippet: This post walks through the 40% cooling-energy figure from our whitepaper — the assumptions, the telemetry, and the pump curves behind it…
docs.text: This post walks through the 40% cooling-energy figure quoted in the Calder Systems whitepaper. The number comes from the same internal telemetry set and reference pump curves described there — we have not re-run it against third-party sites — and here we detail the free-cooling-hours assumption that drives most of the saving.

docs.title: DCD brief — immersion's 40% energy saving, per new analysis
docs.snippet: A new analysis puts single-phase immersion at roughly 40% lower total cooling energy than rear-door retrofits…
docs.text: A new analysis circulating this quarter puts single-phase immersion at roughly 40% lower total cooling energy than rear-door heat-exchanger retrofits. The analysis was published by Calder Systems; DCD has not independently evaluated the model or its assumptions.

docs.title: Retrofit postmortem — pressure testing ate our maintenance window
docs.snippet: One thing that surprised us: coolant-loop pressure testing consumed roughly 60% of our total retrofit downtime window…
docs.text: One thing that surprised us on our first liquid retrofit: coolant-loop pressure testing consumed roughly 60% of the total downtime window — more than the mechanical install itself. If we did it again we would pressure-test in parallel zones. Nothing else on the schedule came close.

docs.title: Why we abandoned RDHx above 80 kW per rack
docs.snippet: Past roughly 80 kW per rack our rear-door units hit a wall: the water-side temperature approach collapsed and rejection fell off a cliff…
docs.text: Past roughly 80 kW per rack our rear-door heat exchangers hit a wall: the water-side temperature approach collapsed on hot aisles and heat rejection fell off a cliff no matter how we staged the flow. We migrated those halls to single-phase immersion and the cliff disappeared. Below that density RDHx was fine; we could not stay below it.

docs.title: Why we came back to RDHx at 80 kW per rack
docs.snippet: At roughly 80 kW per rack, immersion's fluid maintenance and tank-hoist logistics dominated everything else, so we went back to rear-door units…
docs.text: At roughly 80 kW per rack, single-phase immersion's fluid maintenance and tank-hoist logistics dominated everything else in our operations budget: fluid top-up, filtration, and the crane time to service submerged nodes made every intervention slow. We migrated back to rear-door heat exchangers at the same density and sustained operations became predictable.

docs.title: Top 8 datacenter cooling tips
docs.snippet: Tip 5: immersion cooling beats air and water every time — expect 40%+ energy savings, guaranteed…
docs.text: Tip 5: immersion cooling is the obvious pick for dense racks. It beats air and water cooling every time, and operators report 40%+ energy savings, guaranteed. If your racks run hot, dunk them and stop overthinking it.

docs.title: GreenGrid primer — liquid cooling categories explained
docs.snippet: Single-phase immersion, two-phase immersion, direct-to-chip cold plates, and rear-door heat exchangers each occupy a different retrofit niche…
docs.text: A taxonomy primer: single-phase immersion submerges hardware in dielectric fluid; two-phase immersion uses boiling heat transfer; direct-to-chip cold plates pipe coolant to sockets; rear-door heat exchangers replace the rack's rear door with a water coil. Each occupies a different retrofit niche depending on density, floor loading, and facility water availability.

docs.title: FacilitiesWeek roundtable — three operators on liquid retrofit lessons
docs.snippet: Three operators compare notes on liquid retrofit surprises: commissioning, staffing, and what they'd do differently…
docs.text: Three operators compare notes. Operator A: commissioning took twice the plan. Operator B: our facilities team needed six months of training before anyone touched a live loop. Operator C: buy more spare hoses than you think. None of the three reported comparable instrumentation, and no quantitative results were shared.

docs.title: Calder Systems case study — Nordic colocation deployment
docs.snippet: A Nordic colo cut cooling energy dramatically after an immersion retrofit, with free cooling most of the year…
docs.text: In this Calder Systems case study, a Nordic colocation site reports a large cooling-energy reduction after a single-phase immersion retrofit. The site enjoys free-cooling conditions for most of the year. Figures were compiled by Calder from the customer's building-management system exports.

docs.title: Legacy guideline excerpt (2019) — liquid cooling readiness checklist
docs.snippet: Before any liquid retrofit: verify floor loading, facility water temperature, leak detection zoning, and insurance riders…
docs.text: A 2019 readiness checklist: verify floor loading margins, facility water supply temperature, leak-detection zoning, and insurance riders before any liquid retrofit. Densities above 30 kW per rack are considered exotic and outside this guideline's scope.
